messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Maya, a 37-year-old North American musician, came to treatment after months of feeling as though her life had narrowed to the size of the night when the bombing happened. She had been playing a late set with a small venue crowd when the attack hit the district outside the club, and in the chaos that followed she was caught in the crush of bodies, smoke, and sirens, trying to get out through a side door while the air filled with dust and the sharp, metallic taste of blood and debris. What stayed with her most was not a single image but the way the whole scene could return to her in a fully lived way: she would taste that same bitter metal in her mouth, see the details with unbearable clarity, and feel as if she were back in the moment across all her senses at once. Even hearing a muffled explosion in a movie trailer, or the sudden slam of a door near the rehearsal space where she worked, could pull her straight back into that experience, and once the memory began, it often became hard for her to concentrate on the simplest thing in front of her. She described her mind snagging on fragments of the event, as though attention itself were being seized by the memory before she could keep hold of anything else.

In the months that followed, Maya found herself increasingly convinced that the world had changed in a way she could not safely live in. She said she no longer belonged anywhere, that she could not trust people to be what they seemed, and that she had no future she could count on. Those beliefs were not abstract to her; they sharpened each time the memory returned with its unnerving clarity. When the scene came back in full detail, she would be overwhelmed by the sense that she had already seen the true nature of things, that the same violence could appear anywhere and that no setting was reliably safe. At the same time, the more she found herself saying that she was cut off from belonging and doomed to live without a future, the more the event seemed to preserve itself in her mind as proof of those conclusions. She would replay the attack in exact detail, returning over and over to the street, the crowd, the smoke, the taste in her mouth, as if the vividness of the memory could somehow explain why her life now felt permanently unmoored. The memory did not fade with distance; instead, her bleakest beliefs seemed to give it a kind of fuel, making it easier for the scene to come back intact, complete, and terrifyingly real.

What frightened Maya most in daily life was how quickly her body and mind could be thrown back into that state. At rehearsals and gigs, she watched the exits, checked the crowd, and found herself scanning for anything unusual, especially in crowded rooms or when loud noises cut through the music. A backfiring car outside the studio, a sudden crash from the kitchen of the bar where she sometimes played, or the echo of a bass note through the floor could leave her briefly disoriented, irritable, and unable to keep her thoughts on the set list. She had started snapping at her partner over small things because she felt keyed up and on edge, then felt ashamed of the outbursts without being able to stop them next time. She also began avoiding certain venues and turning down work that took her into packed spaces, telling herself she was being practical, though the cost was that her world grew smaller and her career less stable. Friends noticed she was more absent in conversation, losing track of what they were saying and then apologizing, embarrassed by how hard it had become to follow even ordinary exchanges when the memory intruded or her attention went thin with vigilance.

By the time she sought help, Maya was exhausted by the way the event kept reclaiming her life. She wanted to keep playing music, but she was afraid that one more sudden sound, one more crowded room, would bring the whole experience back with such force that she would lose control in public. What finally brought her in was realizing that she was spending more energy avoiding reminders than living, and that the beliefs she had come to accept about not belonging anywhere and having no future were beginning to feel like the only truth she knew.
